# Urbanization and childhood asthma

**Authors:** Teresia T. Pham; Yeside Akinbolagbe; Thinh H. Nguyen; Wanda Phipatanakul

**Affiliations:** 1Division of Immunology, Boston Children’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 2Department of Pediatrics, Tufts School of Medicine, Boston, MA, USA | 3Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 4Atrius Health, Medford, MA, USA

## Abstract

Childhood asthma is one of the major public health concerns, and urbanization as well as worsening environmental factors are contributing to its increasing prevalence. Outdoor pollutants, such as PM2.5, ozone, and traffic-related air pollution or TRAP, play significant roles in exacerbating asthmatic symptoms in children as well as reducing their lung function. Climate change can further compound these effects with changing pollen patterns that increase exposure to allergens in certain geographical areas. Moreover, indoor environments in urban areas also expose children to pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide, particulate matter, and aeroallergens like cockroach or mouse allergens. Socioeconomic disparities can further amplify these effects, with children in minority or low-income households disproportionately burdened by asthma morbidity. Green infrastructure and technological innovations can offer mitigation opportunities for negative effects of urbanization but require careful implementation to address multifactorial contributors to childhood asthma. Our review highlights the need for integrated strategies regarding environmental regulation, urban planning, and targeted interventions to reduce asthma burden in urban pediatric population.

## Introduction:

Asthma is one of the most common chronic diseases in children.1 The current global rise in childhood asthma has been closely linked to urbanization and its environmental consequences.2 The disconnection of humans from contact with soil microorganisms caused by urbanization has also been hypothesized to be an important factor responsible for the current asthma or atopy epidemic via its disruption of immunologic homeostasis. The high population density, industrial activity, traffic, and worsening air quality in urban areas are the key drivers of asthma exacerbation.3 Climate change further exacerbates these factors.4 Poor indoor environment in urban areas also poses additional risks for children with asthma with exposure to allergens such as mold, cockroach, and mouse allergens.5 Socioeconomic factors such as crowded housing, lack of healthcare access, and psychological stress can further burden children in low-income households.6 Our review examines how urbanization shapes indoor and outdoor environmental exposures, as well as socioeconomic conditions, all of which contribute to asthma risk and morbidity in children (Figure I).

### Outdoor environment and asthma

#### Environmental factors – air quality and pollution

The expansion of urbanization has led to increasing emissions from vehicles, industrial activities, and construction. Consequently, air pollution intensifies over time, and the accompanying climate change exacerbates conditions such as wildfires, extreme temperatures, and more severe and longer pollen seasons. These factors emerge as significant outdoor environmental contributors to the increasing prevalence of childhood asthma and allergic diseases.

Air pollution is a mixture of various pollutants, composing of gaseous and particulate matter. Gaseous pollutants include nitrogen dioxide (NO2), sulfur dioxide (SO2), carbon monoxide (CO), carbon dioxide (CO2), and heavy metals such as lead and chromium.7–10 Particulate matter is classified by size, PM10 for particles of 10 micrometers or less, and PM2.5 for particles of 2.5 micrometers or less. PM2.5 can penetrate deep into the lungs and blood stream, causing adverse effects in multiple body organ systems.11 Research has shown that children exposed to PM2.5 or smaller are at risk for further aggravating respiratory symptoms and reduced lung function.11,12 Particulate matter is known to have the greatest impact on human health and is frequently used as a key indicator of air quality.7

Ozone is a notable pollutant known to cause inflammation in the airways, exacerbating asthma symptoms and increasing respiratory infections in children.13 Ground-level ozone (O₃) is formed when pollutants like nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), which are released from vehicles, power plants, and industrial facilities, undergo chemical reactions in the presence of sunlight.14 TRAP, which is composed of gaseous and particulate matter, has been of particular interest to study in the development and worsening of asthma.7–10 There is growing evidence of children living close to traffic areas having worsening asthma symptoms or new asthma symptoms.15 A study conducted following The Cincinnati Childhood Allergy and Air Pollution Study (CCAAPS) examined early childhood exposure to TRAP before 12 months of age suggests that there is an increased risk of persistent wheezing at 36 months of age.10 The Children’s Health Study (CHS) in Southern California, which examined >11,000 children in twelve communities, has been pivotal in understanding long-term effects of air pollution on children’s respiratory health.16 Key findings from the study showed that exposure to the four pollutants, NO2, PM2.5, acid vapor, and O3, was linked to impaired lung development in children.16,17 The study also found that the effect on lung function in children ages 10 – 18, as measured by changes in FEV₁, appeared to be similar in magnitude to the impact associated with maternal smoking exposure.17 Conversely, as air quality improved in California due to stricter regulations, a study found that the incidence of asthma subsequently decreased.18 Other areas in North America have also experienced much of the same deleterious effects of industrialization. For example, a retrospective study in Mexico City examined emergency visits from January to June 1990 at a well-known pediatric hospital found that exposure to elevated ozone levels was linked to a 68% increase in asthma-related emergency visits for children.19

#### Climate and weather in urban spaces

Urbanization additionally affects climate change. The interplay between air pollution and climate change is critical as they both share common sources and have reinforcing effects. Climate change appears to alter allergenic pollen patterns, both by lengthening pollen seasons and by increasing allergen concentrations. Higher temperatures and CO₂ levels intensify pollen production, with urban heat islands amplifying these effects in city areas. Increased pollen levels correlate with higher rates of asthma and allergies, as they heighten sensitization and immune responses.20 Ren et al. created a model to analyze how major pollen allergens, including oak and ragweed, are distributed across the contiguous United States (CONUS) over time. Their simulation spans both historical data (2004) and projected future conditions (2047). The findings reveal significant regional differences in pollen metrics, with ragweed seasons predicted to begin earlier and extend longer in all climate zones, and oak pollen seasons displaying notable variability in both timing and intensity across regions with the largest increases in pollen concentrations predicted in the Northeast.21 On a similar note, a study done using the growing degree hour (GDH) model gathering data from six stations in the US from 1994 to 2011 showed birch and oak trees flower 1–2 weeks earlier with the annual average and peak value of daily pollen concentrations increasing by 13.6%−248%.22

Climate-driven weather changes, such as more frequent heatwaves and wildfires, lead to the release of particulates and allergens. These changes deteriorate air quality and extreme heat can compromise epithelial barriers and immune function, further exacerbating asthma risk.12,23 Extreme heat and precipitation events are of particular importance due to elevated risks for asthma exacerbation. A study done in Maryland between the years 2000 – 2012 showed summertime extreme heat event had the highest risk of asthma hospitalization in ages 5 – 17 years.24 The effects of extreme temperatures and wildfires also reaches other sparsely populated areas. In the rural and intermountain region of Western Montana in the US, a study conducted showed the impact of PM2.5 on respiratory health varied with temperature extremes.25 This region of the US often has increased exposure to PM2.5 due to residential wood burning during the winter and smoke from surrounding wildfires during the summer.26 The study found that exposure to PM2.5 during the colder months increased the incidence of asthma and lower respiratory tract infections, whereas during the hotter months, there was an increase in the upper respiratory tract infections.25

These trends highlight the importance of implementing comprehensive strategies to alleviate the health impacts of urbanization and climate change in children, including urban planning to increase green spaces for improved air quality and public health initiatives aimed at reducing emissions and managing allergen exposure.

#### Genetics and Epigenetic factors

In addition to environmental and psychosocial factors, genetic and epigenetic mechanisms are increasingly recognized as important contributors to asthma pathogenesis.27 Urban stressors such as air pollution, maternal stress, and socioeconomic adversity can lead to epigenetic modifications including DNA methylation and histone changes that influence immune system development and airway inflammation. These changes can affect asthma susceptibility even in early life, including in utero, and may help explain intergenerational differences in asthma burden among children living in urban environments.28,29 Understanding these gene-environment interactions is essential for developing targeted prevention strategies.

#### Nature-based solutions and their effect on asthma

Nature-based solutions (NbS), such as green infrastructure, biodiversity-promoting urban design, and low-allergen vegetation planning, are increasingly implemented in cities worldwide to improve air quality and respiratory health outcomes.30,31 Urban green infrastructure has been shown to reduce urban heat islands local air pollution and the stresses of climate change. Urban heat islands refer to areas that have distinctly higher temperatures than their surrounding rural areas.32 Green infrastructure includes elements such as street trees and parks for shade and cooling, urban lakes and rivers, hedges, green roofs and walls, and agricultural fields.33 These elements offer not only a wide range of economic, social, and psychological benefits for the community, but can also improve air quality and regulate the local climate.30,34 For example, increasing street trees in New York City have been shown to decrease asthma symptoms in children.8 A recent study by Feleszko et. al investigated the association between early exposure to residential greenness and the development of asthma in children hospitalized for severe bronchiolitis. The research suggests that exposure to residential greenness may offer protective benefits against asthma development in children by age six, particularly those with early respiratory infections such as severe bronchiolitis, a known risk factor for asthma development.35 A large population-based cohort study in Ontario, Canada, also showed that higher residential greenness may reduce the risk of developing asthma in children aged 7 to 12. Unfortunately, studies on the benefits of residential greenness for respiratory health have yielded mixed results, as some have found instead that increased pollen exposure from vegetation may worsen asthma symptoms and trigger allergic reactions.36 Nonetheless, efforts are underway to guide urban planning by considering the allergenicity of plants. Certain tools have been proposed to help identify plants with lower allergenic potential to create healthier public spaces.37

#### Mitigation strategies for the effect of urbanization on asthma (Table 1)

In the United States, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) was created in 1970 to safeguard human health and the environment.38 Congress also passed the Clean Air Act (CAA) to regulate air pollution with amendments made over the years to enhance public health protections.39 Under the CAA, the EPA could set and enforce the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS), regulate emissions of hazardous air pollutants such as O3, monitor air quality and ensure compliance with the law, as well as addressing acid rain, ozone depletion, and greenhouse gas emissions.39,40 The Clean Air Act (CAA) has resulted in decreased ozone concentrations over the last several decades.41 However, a significant number of the U.S. population continues to be exposed to air pollution levels that exceed the current NAAQS set by the EPA.42

Technological innovations are on the rise in helping to decrease and manage respiratory symptoms in children. Mobile apps on Apple or Android phones can help track air quality and provide teaching and training information for asthma control.43 Smart inhalers can ensure optimal medication delivery by providing feedback on user technique, tracking medication usage, checking medication load, and providing reminders.44 Limitations of app usage include their clinical efficacy, privacy and security when putting in personal information.45,46

Additionally, emerging evidence suggests that certain diets may play a protective role against asthma development and severity. Diets rich in fruits, vegetables, omega-3 fatty acids, and whole grain, such as the Mediterranean diets, have been correlated with reduced systemic inflammation and improved respiratory health.47,48 High fiber intake may also modulate the gut microbiome and promote the production of short-chain fatty acids, which can enhance immune regulation and reduce airway inflammation.49 Incorporating nutritional approaches into public health strategies could offer a complementary pathway for mitigating the impact of urbanization on childhood asthma.

There are other challenges in proposing ways to decrease air pollution. For example, hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) propellants in certain metered dose inhalers (pMDIs) such as Flovent and albuterol HFA (a type of HFC), have a high global warming potential (GWP) and stay around the Earth’s atmosphere longer.50 The shift toward reducing the use of HFC propellants in steroid inhalers to lower the carbon footprint could negatively impact pediatric asthma care. Children under 5 years old are unlikely to effectively use alternatives like dry powder inhalers (DPIs), which require stronger inhalation and breath-holding. This limitation may lead to inadequate delivery of steroid doses, increasing the risk of asthma exacerbations. As a result, these children rely more on rescue albuterol HFA inhalers, potentially generating a higher carbon footprint overall.50,51

### Indoor environment and asthma

The indoor environment, including both home and school settings, along with air quality and exposures, plays a significant role in asthma incidence and morbidity among children living in urban areas. Children are more susceptible to indoor exposures as they tend to spend about 90% of their time indoors with about 6–8 hours a day at school.52 Urbanization, which leads to crowded housing due to limited space, with many families living in poorly ventilated apartment buildings with limited outdoor play areas, potentiates the effects of indoor exposures. A study by Keet et al that evaluated about 17 million children enrolled in Medicaid over 1 year confirmed that living in an urban or poor area posed significantly greater risks for asthma related emergency department (ED) visits and hospitalizations. It was found that children with asthma residing in nonurban areas had 18% to 28% lower risk of hospitalizations compared to those living in urban areas, even after controlling for race/ethnicity. However urban residential status did not have a significant effect on asthma prevalence.53

Research studies done in the US, have shown that the inner-city home environment with airborne pollutants, aeroallergens and mold exposures are associated with significant asthma morbidity.54,55 Asthma severity can also be modified by various environmental factors which include pollutants such as particulate matter (PM), nitrogen oxides, secondhand smoke, and allergens from pests, pets, and molds.56 The common indoor air pollutants include products of combustion, including particulate matter (PM) and oxides of nitrogen, airborne allergens and endotoxin.54

#### Indoor air pollution and asthma

A longitudinal study of 150 inner city preschool children with asthma, a part of the Johns Hopkins Center for Childhood Asthma (Baltimore Indoor Environment Study of Asthma in Kids [BIESAK] Study) found high concentrations of NO2, fine particles- PM 2.5, and coarse particles- P.M 5 and PM10 in their homes and bedrooms. Significant determinants of indoor PM concentrations included smoking, sweeping, and stove use activities. The study also suggested that smoking could be a significant contributor to PM exposure in the inner city, finding differences in PM 2.5 of 26 μg/m3 between smoking and nonsmoking households.54

Timing of exposure to indoor air pollution has been identified to be an important factor in asthma development. Early prenatal exposure to tobacco was associated with higher asthma risk at 7 years of age in a birth cohort of 442 high-risk inner-city children from The Urban Environment and Childhood Asthma (URECA) Study.57 Umbilical cord plasma cotinine concentration was 76% higher in children diagnosed with asthma. This has also been corroborated in a recent study in which pregnancy was identified as the critical time period of home environmental exposure associated with asthma development, especially for exposure to environmental tobacco smoke (ETS), new furniture, mold/damp clothes and bedding with increased odds of 39–55%.58 A metanalysis of 13 studies evaluating the impact of postnatal environmental tobacco smoke ETS (combustion smoke and vaping) on risk of new-onset asthma, reported an increased risk of 12%, with stronger associations observed when both parents smoked. ETS exposure was also linked to a three-fold increase in odds of asthma-related ED visits in children with asthma.59

In a subset of children from our longitudinal cohort study of urban school aged children with asthma in Northeastern US, the School Inner-city Asthma Study (SICAS), tobacco biomarkers; urinary cotinine and total 4-(methylnitrosamino)-1-(3-pyridyl)-1-butanol (NNAL) levels; were independently associated with asthma morbidity. For every log10 increase in cotinine level, there was a 34.7% increased odds of hospitalization over the previous year and a 172% increased odds of hospitalization for every log10 increase in NNAL level.60

Residing near busy roads significantly increases exposure to a variety of air pollutants and noise generated by vehicles, including particulate matter, mobile source air toxicants like benzene, nitrogen oxides, hydrocarbons, and carbon monoxide.61 Children living in urban areas are more likely to live or school in close proximity to major roads. Hansel and colleagues reported that about 71% of children in the BIESAK longitudinal cohort lived within 25 ft of the street.62 A study in California found that a substantial number of children attended public schools in urban areas close to major roads with very high traffic counts, and a disproportionate number of those students were economically disadvantaged and nonwhite.63 Furthermore, the SICAS cohort, demonstrated that proximity (within 100ft) to major roadways, using a composite measurement of both home and school exposure, was associated with increased asthma symptoms, health care utilization, and poor asthma control.64 Another school-based study done in the SICAS cohort also reported that ambient nitrogen dioxide levels in inner-city schools was associated with worse outcomes in students with asthma.65

The National Cooperative Inner City Asthma Study (NCICAS) conducted in eight inner cities across the United States had previously shown a link between higher concentrations of indoor NO2 and increased symptoms and decreased peak expiratory flows in children with asthma.66 Thus, highlighting the important contribution of the indoor school environment to childhood asthma in urban areas.

Recent studies by our research group in school children with asthma living in Northeastern US urban areas have identified an association between radon exposure and increased risk for asthma. Moreover, our study also found elevated fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO), a marker of airway inflammation, in children exposed to residential radon levels, even when the radon level is below the current safety thresholds.67,68

#### Aeroallergens and biological exposures

Exposure to allergens from cockroaches and mice is common, particularly in lower-income urban communities, and contributes to increased asthma morbidity. It has been previously reported that the concentration of mouse allergen varies as much as 1000-fold between inner-city and non-inner-city environments.69 Pest allergen sensitization to mouse and cockroach allergens was associated with a higher odds of asthma exacerbations in urban minority youth from the Genes-environments and Admixture in Latino American (GALA-II) and Study of African-Americans, Asthma, Genes, and Environments (SAGE-II) study cohorts.70 In the BIESAK cohort, about 100% of the inner city Baltimore homes had detectable mouse allergen in settled dust samples as well as airborne mouse allergen detected in greater than 80% of the bedrooms sampled. Furthermore, both asthma symptoms and asthma-related health care use were more common among mouse sensitized participants who had greater than 0.5mg/g of mouse allergen in their bedroom dust sample than in the others. The associations between mouse allergen exposure and asthma outcomes were found to be independent of cockroach sensitization/exposure, public health insurance, atopy, age, and sex.71,72

Low-income households in the US have been found to be 12 times as likely to have high cockroach allergen (> 8 U/g) compared to households with high income.73–75 In The National Cooperative Inner-City Asthma Study, children in the US sensitized and exposed to cockroach were 3.4 times more likely to be hospitalized.76 Classroom-specific exposure to mouse allergen, was demonstrated in inner city schools by the SICAS study. It was found that in inner-city school-aged children with asthma, exposure to higher levels of school mouse allergen was associated with a higher number of days with asthma symptoms and decreased lung function, independent of home environmental exposure. This effect was also seen regardless of mouse sensitization, further strengthening the evidence of the impact of school exposures on asthma morbidity in inner cities.77 Children in racial and ethnic minority urban communities living in houses of poor quality and disrepair are at increased risk of exposure to mold.78 Mold exposure is associated with childhood wheeze, asthma prevalence and morbidity.79–82 Among 41,423 children in the 2017–2018 National Surveys of Children’s Health (NSCH) study, the prevalence of current asthma was 11.9% in mold-exposed children, compared to 8.2% in non-exposed children. Furthermore, children with household mold exposure compared to those with no household mold exposure had a 1.41-fold higher odds of current asthma, which was more pronounced among boys.83 In The Asthma Phenotypes in the Inner-City study which recruited children, aged 6 to 17 years, from 8 US cities living in urban areas, the average concentration of the mold “Mucor” was significantly higher in homes of children with difficult to control asthma particularly in those with window air conditioning which fosters its growth.55 Outdoor mold-exposure in schools has also been found to be significantly higher compared with homes in the SICAS cohort. Most of the schools were thought to be predisposed to this due to absence of air-conditioning. The presence of air-conditioning in school buildings was associated with lower asthma prevalence.84

Dust allergen and endotoxin levels in urban areas are high and contribute to asthma morbidity. The National Survey of Lead and Allergens in Housing (NSLAH) study which assayed endotoxin from 2,552 house dust samples found major predictors of endotoxin concentration were sampling location in the home, census division, educational attainment, presence of children, current dog ownership, resident-described problems with cockroaches, food debris, cockroach stains, and evidence of smoking observed by field staff.85 Furthermore, Mendy et al in a study of over 6000 participants also found clustering of endotoxin with allergens in dust from homes with pets or of people with low socioeconomic status which was associated with a 42% and 32% higher prevalence of asthma and wheeze respectively.86 Thus, eliciting the interplay between different indoor exposures and their synergistic influence on asthma.

#### Effects of socio-economic factors associated with urbanization on asthma

Social disparities exist which make the effects of urbanization on asthma more pronounced in children of low socioeconomic status living in inner-cities or urban areas.87 Studies have shown that these minority children have a disproportionately higher burden of asthma morbidity. The study by Keet et al showed that among a population of low-income children with asthma, black race and living in poor areas were significant independent risk factors for ED visits and hospitalization. Children with these risk factors, had 89% and 10% higher risk of hospitalization respectively, compared to those without.53

Social determinants of health (SDOH) in children have been quantified using the child opportunity index (COI) which is a composite index combining multiple indicators of neighborhood advantage into a single score for each census tract in the USA using data from the largest 100 metropolitan areas. The COI is comprised of 44 indicators across three domains (education, health and environment, and social and economic) and 14 subdomains with higher COI reflecting higher opportunity.88 This standardized measure captures neighborhood “opportunity” defined as “neighborhood-based conditions and resources conducive to healthy child development.89 Some studies have found COI to be associated with various asthma outcomes. A recent secondary analysis of 2 observational studies done in Colorado, reported that a 20-point COI decrease conferred 40% higher odds of exacerbation-prone asthma.90

Lower opportunity has also been linked with asthma-related emergency visits and hospitalization rates, longer hospital stays and more pediatric ICU admissions.91–93 There are disparities in availability and quality of asthma healthcare particularly in low income, minority urban communities. Factors, such as lack of health insurance, access to primary care, and fewer referrals to asthma specialists, all result in higher ER utilization for asthma, increased school and work absences, decreased provider consistency, uncontrolled asthma, and overall worse asthma care”.94,95 Another study also reported that patients with asthma who were on public insurance were less likely to be treated with biologics even when indicated.96

Stress in inner cities from exposure to violence, crime, poverty with associated lack of basic needs and nutrition all contribute to increased asthma development and morbidity.94 In the Urban Environment and Childhood asthma study across 4 US cities, in which mothers were recruited from areas with > 20% of residents living below the poverty level, maternal exposure to prenatal stress was associated with altered innate and immune responses in cord blood mononuclear cells. This was postulated to impact the development of allergic disease in their children.97 This finding has been corroborated by a summary of systematic reviews and metanalysis of studies providing evidence establishing that there is an increased risk of asthma with exposure to psychosocial stress, particularly during the prenatal and early postnatal period.98

Children exposed to high levels of chronic stress have been reported to have increased asthma exacerbations, decreased asthma control, increased hospitalizations, decreased quality of life, and decreased lung function.99–101 A study in children with asthma in New orleans, Louisiana reported that those with exposure to both cockroaches and caregivers with high stress levels, had increased odds of unscheduled clinic/ED visits and hospitalizations.102

#### Interventions to mitigate indoor allergen exposure, air pollution and socioeconomic factors.

Many interventions aimed at reducing allergen exposure and air pollution to improve indoor environments in urban inner cities and mitigate their impact on childhood asthma have evolved over the years, achieving varying levels of success. One of the earliest prominent studies, the inner-city asthma study (ICAS),103 conducted across 7 US Cities among children with atopic asthma, investigated an individualized home-based comprehensive environmental intervention over a one-year period. It successfully decreased indoor allergens, including cockroach and dust-mite allergens which resulted in reduction of asthma symptom days, unscheduled ED or clinic visits for asthma and hospitalizations compared to the control group and these effects were sustained for up to one year after the intervention. The intervention combined the use of allergen-impermeable covers for beds and pillows, vacuum cleaners with high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters, HEPA air purifiers in children’s bedrooms, and professional pest control.

A randomized control trial by our research group,104 conducted in 18 Boston inner-city homes of children with asthma, was one of the first to demonstrate the effectiveness of integrated pest management in reducing mouse allergen levels. We used an integrated pest management strategy, which consisted of filling holes and cracks, setting traps, vacuuming with HEPA filters, cleaning surfaces with mild detergents, dusting wall voids and pipe chases with low-toxicity pesticides, and educating the family on pest control measures. This was performed in a standardized fashion by professional exterminators. The study found that mouse allergen levels significantly decreased by 79% in homes of the intervention group, compared with the control group, where allergen levels increased by > 300% by the end of the 5-month intervention period. There was, however, no significant effect on asthma outcomes and lung function, which was probably due to the small sample size. Similar results of no difference in asthma symptoms were obtained in the Mouse Allergen and Asthma Intervention Trial (MAAIT)105 which compared an intensive, professionally delivered, integrated pest management (IPM) home intervention in addition to education about pest management with education alone, among mouse-sensitized and exposed children and adolescents with persistent asthma. These findings were thought to be attributed to the IPM intervention, not being associated with substantially larger decreases in home mouse allergen levels. Furthermore, the pest management education alone group (control group) had large decreases in home mouse allergen levels of approximately 65%, which is larger than that obtained in prior home intervention studies among the active intervention group. However, a large, controlled trial of a mouse allergen environmental intervention,106 in a subset of the population from the ICAS study, obtained a reduction in mouse allergen levels which was associated with significantly decreased caregiver burden, child sleep disruption, and missed school days after controlling for cockroach allergen exposure and sensitivity.

Interventions to improve home indoor air quality, such as using HEPA air cleaners and a health coach, have shown varying effects on asthma outcomes, including reducing unscheduled asthma visits and asthma symptoms, as well as improving asthma control in children living in inner cities who are exposed to secondhand tobacco smoke and traffic-related airborne particles.107–109 Our study, the School-based Inner-city Asthma Intervention Study (SICAS II),110 a randomized, blinded, sham-controlled school environmental intervention trial, attempted to demonstrate the effect of two interventions, integrated pest management (IPM) in schools and HEPA air filters in classrooms. There was no significant reduction in the primary outcome, symptom days with asthma, between either of the 2 interventions and control groups. However, IPM led to a significant reduction in asthma symptoms during the early postintervention period (fall and winter), though these effects were not sustained later in the school year. There was also a significant reduction in the number of missed school days due to asthma in the school-wide IPM group, which may help to reduce the burden of asthma on children and their families. On the other hand, HEPA filters effectively reduced exposures but did not reduce asthma symptom days. The school IPM plus classroom HEPA intervention was shown to be cost-effective.111 We have also identified disparities in school teachers across different school regions, suggesting school wide interventions can benefit a community of students and staff as opposed to individual families in single homes.112 Furthermore, in post-hoc analysis, students who had higher mold exposure at school compared to home, showed improved lung function with classroom HEPA filters.113 This suggests that certain subgroups of students may benefit from these interventions, but it is difficult to determine health effects on larger populations in a school setting. Moreover, classroom HEPA filters reduced airborne allergens which is a step towards improving asthma morbidity. The difference in asthma health outcomes compared to home-based studies may be attributed to the short length of time of the IPM and difficulties in sustaining the effects of interventions in large environments like schools.

Currently, our group has initiated the PARK (Preventing Asthma in High-Risk Kids) study, a randomized controlled trial investigating whether early intervention with omalizumab, an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody, can prevent the progression of asthma in high-risk, school-aged children.114 The study aims to block IgE responses to environmental allergens in children aged 2–3 years with a history of wheezing and significant atopic risk, evidenced by allergic sensitization, to potentially modify the disease trajectory. Based on our previous studies on the effect of radon on asthma67,68, we are going to conduct the Radon Asthma Intervention Trial (ROME) (NCT06706336),115 which is a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial designed to investigate the efficacy of radon mitigation in the homes of susceptible individuals. The trial aims to provide evidence of the health benefits of improving indoor air quality by mitigating the negative effect of radon on children with asthma. We are planning to recruit 180 children with asthma then a standard radon-specific mitigation system will be installed in the participants’ homes. Health outcomes will be monitored over 48 weeks to evaluate the effect of the intervention versus the sham control.

Multi-faceted interventions are necessary to improve neighborhood advantages and mitigate the negative effects of socioeconomic factors on asthma in children living in urban areas, as relocating families from their living situations may not always be feasible. This will require collaborative efforts and policies from government agencies and the private sector to address historical and structural racism, which has disproportionately affected minority communities. These communities often face poor housing, poverty, inequities in access to education and employment, greater exposure to pests, mold, and air pollution, disparities in healthcare access and quality, and high levels of chronic stress.94 Some success has been seen in recent studies in the US. A cohort study of 123 children aged 5 to 17 years with persistent asthma whose families participated in the Baltimore Regional Housing Partnership housing mobility program that provided housing vouchers and assistance moving to low-poverty neighborhoods was associated with significantly reduced odds of asthma exacerbations and asthma symptoms.116 Furthermore, measures of stress, including social cohesion, neighborhood safety, and urban stress, all improved with moving and mediated this association by about 29% to 35%. Male children and children at a higher asthma controller medication treatment step had a greater reduction in maximum symptom days with moving.117

We have advocated for the implementation of School-supervised asthma therapy (SST),118 an evidence-based intervention previously demonstrated to improve preventive medication adherence and asthma symptoms for children from historically marginalized backgrounds, as a strategy to reduce long standing inequities in asthma morbidity.

## Conclusion:

In summary, our review provides an integrated analysis of how urbanization contributes to childhood asthma through a combination of outdoor and indoor environmental exposures, socioeconomic disparities, and structural inequities. Unlike prior studies that focus on individual factors, our work emphasizes the importance of a multidimensional framework that includes both environmental and social determinants of health. Based on this synthesis, we recommend several policy and public health strategies: (1) expand environmental regulations to address indoor air quality, particularly in low-income housing and schools; (2) incorporate allergen-aware green infrastructure and low-emission urban planning into asthma prevention policies; and (3) invest in school-based interventions, such as supervised therapy, stress management and indoor environmental controls, targeting high-risk communities. These integrated strategies are critical to reducing the asthma burden and promoting health equity in urban settings.
